cipher-grid.intro_html:
Polygraphia VI (1550, Frankfurt) -- Cipher-grid tables (Style C)

Source witness: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (BSB) München, via MDZ digital library. Contains the Clavis Polygraphiae bound in.

What you are looking at

These chunks render Trithemius's tabular ciphers -- structurally different from the verbal-substitution columns of the cipher-key set. Three families recur:

  • Expansion-figure matrices (Prima / Secunda / Tertia / Quarta figura expansionis tabulae) -- bigram-pair tables and alphabet-rotation grids that derive new alphabets from a base alphabet by transposition.
  • Orchema numerale -- a 24x24 numerical-substitution matrix in Polygraphia VI book six, indexed by Latin letters on both axes with numbers 6-29 in the body. Trithemius's own note describes the diagonals as an 'infinite leap' (transversaliter a quatuor angulis).
  • Spirit-army hierarchies -- positional tables of demonic ranks (Oriens / Duxes majoris / Duxes minoris / Subduces) from the Steganographia tradition; structurally tabular but not a cipher in the strict substitution-table sense.

How the renderer chose its layout

Each source section is tokenised row-by-row. When most rows have the same cell count (and that count is <= 28), the renderer emits a markdown table; otherwise it preserves the source layout as a fenced code block. Trithemius's own commentary (where it appears in long Latin prose between figures) is lifted out into a blockquote. -- marks an OCR-illegible cell.

Honest limits

  • Identical-rows artefact: the printed Polygraphia VI expansion figures display Caesar-rotated alphabets, but the OCR frequently linearises them to identical rows (each row = the plain alphabet). The renderer surfaces what the OCR sees; the original rotation is recoverable only by inspecting the facsimile image.
  • Header detection is heuristic: lines matching figure-header patterns are lifted out, but a header buried in continuous prose may be missed.
  • This work contributes 15 cipher-grid chunks.

Provenance

Auto-generated from the OCR'd source by scripts/render_style_cipher_grid.py. Phase 0.5 manual reclassification moved 43 expansion-figure chunks from cipher-key to cipher-grid (see scripts/reclassify_expansion_figures.py).

cipher-key.intro_html:
Polygraphia VI (1550, Frankfurt) — Cipher tables

Source witness: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (BSB) München, via MDZ digital library. Contains the Clavis Polygraphiae bound in.

What you are looking at

The Polygraphia VI is Johannes Trithemius's exposition of substitution cipher technique, originally dedicated to Maximilian I in 1508. Each of the six books presents a different modus of enciphering plaintext as a sequence of Latin words. The basic mechanism is constant across modi:

  • The plaintext is broken into individual letters.
  • Each letter is replaced by a Latin word drawn from a substitution column (the alphabetum of cipher words).
  • For multi-column modi, the substitution rotates with the letter's position: position 1 uses column 1, position 2 uses column 2, and so on, returning to column 1 once the sequence exhausts.
  • The cipher words are chosen so that any ordinary plaintext produces a grammatical Latin sentence — invariably a devotional invocation. The ciphertext is thus undetectable: it reads as ordinary monastic prayer.

Worked example — Modus Primus, eight-column substitution

To encipher the eight-letter plaintext ABCDEFGH using Modus Primus (the first cipher of Liber Septimus / Clavis Polygraphiae, eight substitution columns):

pos plain col cipher-word
1 A C1 facti
2 B C2 Certe
3 C C3 timendum
4 D C4 continue
5 E C5 sempiternum
6 F C6 fabricatorem
7 G C7 supercaelestium
8 H C8 compassionem

The resulting ciphertext reads:

Facti certe timendum continue sempiternum fabricatorem supercaelestium compassionem.

"[We have] truly been made, [to be] continually feared the eternal fashioner of the heavenly ones, by compassion."

To an eavesdropper this is an ordinary Latin devotional sentence. Only the recipient who knows to take the n-th letter of the n-th word's enciphering column recovers the plaintext ABCDEFGH.

How to read the table files

The substitution columns from this work's source are rendered per chunk under translations/style-c-cipher-key/full/. This work contributes 68 cipher-key chunks; 64 parse cleanly into Style C tables and 4 fall back to a verbatim source rendering (see Honest limits below).

Each chunk file:

  • Identifies the source chunk (e.g. full_chunk_0025).
  • States the per-page-section detected patterns:
  • A — one entry per line (single substitution column, or several columns concatenated on one page).
  • B — two or three columns interleaved per line (a X a Y or a X a Y a Z), with optional trailing source line-numbers.
  • D — letter plus several numeric cipher values per line.
  • Renders an alphabet-down / columns-across markdown table aligned by Trithemius's 24-letter alphabet (a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t v x y z w, omitting j and u), plus an optional 25th zu / zv / tv slot for the v-ligature.

Honest limits

  • OCR scannos are preserved as-they-appear in cell values (e.g. Vtigiz for Vtique, fabricatosem for fabricatorem, pissislimum for piissimum). The v1 parser repairs positional OCR errors in the letter markers (long-s misread as f; 2v misread for zv; iv/lv for zv) but does not repair content — that is a translation-quality problem (handled by the GPT-5.5 audit pipeline), not a layout problem.
  • Dropped column markers: where a row had its column marker dropped by OCR (e.g. a misericordislima factorem instead of a misericordislima a factorem), the parser splits the value into N equal pieces when N matches the section's modal cells-per-row, and leaves the value merged otherwise.
  • Letter-marker repair via positional alignment: when a column is near-full (≥ 18 entries), each entry's letter marker is rewritten to its positional canonical alphabet slot. This catches the common long-s/f confusion (where row s was rendered as f by the OCR) but assumes the column traverses the alphabet sequentially from a.
  • Wide multi-alphabet tables: a subset of chunks (4 of 68 for this work) hold very wide octo-modus tables that the v1 parser cannot sub-split into individual columns. These fall back to a verbatim rendering of the source OCR, with a comment indicating the parser's limit.

Provenance

Auto-generated from the OCR'd source by scripts/render_style_cipher_key.py and scripts/build_cipher_book_intro.py. The OCR pipeline, manual chunk reclassification (Phase 0.5), and GPT-5.5 audit are documented in data/corpus/_PHASE_05_FINDINGS.md and METHODOLOGY_GPT_AUDIT.md. This Style C rendering is one of the four content-type rendering styles chosen for the crypto-occult cluster after the 2026-05-30 Phase 1 specimen review.

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: mid_damage_recoverable; OCR quality: 4/5.

Audit note — V1.0 smoothed several damaged loci into fluent certainty, especially praemalitudine, sine repta, and the broken philosophical clause on finite number.

Polygraphia VI, Back-Matter: Straight Table of Transposition

Transposition Instructions

You will have transmitted [it]. First, indeed, let the first alphabet^1 be assigned first, the second second, the third third, and so let it be done successively with the rest. But if, [conjectured: because of the multitude]^2 of business or of the household, the alphabets which we have marked out should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too exposed and manifest, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions,^3 of which the number may be very great, and the method of the secret^4 may remain always perpetually hidden.

Let us set down an example of this matter: let b be a, f be b, l be c, p be d, t be e, z be f, c be g, m be h, and so successively through the whole usual alphabet,^5 so that between any letter taken up three idle^6 and transposed letters [conjectured: lie between].^7 Afterward four, then [conjectured: five], more or fewer, yet in such a way that the whole alphabet, as though revolved into a circle, comes together, and no letter at all is omitted, but each single one is placed in the same series for another in its own order. In whatever manner you write it, you must know that it is to be firmly committed either to written letters or to memory, lest, having slipped through forgetfulness, you yourself can no longer read what you had written.

For the transposition of letters can be varied in as many ways as, according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed by temporal operation in a mortal body, does not grasp [unclear] and finite [things], an innumerable number for mortal man will arise. Therefore whoever wishes to have more methods of writing by metathesis^8, and methods removed from our instruction, if he is even a little ingenious and diligent, will easily obtain the effect in his operation. For talent can do very great things if it is aided by study and art. But he who despises the smallest things will never reach the greater. I know that there will be very many who will mock these studies of ours as vain and childish; to them we give this as an answer: that we shall be entirely content, provided only that they please those at whose request they were composed by us.

The straight table follows.

OCR praemalitudine is best read as prae multitudine, “because of the multitude”; a typical spacing/letter confusion rather than authorial obscurity. ^3. transpositiones: systematic substitutions or rearrangements of letters in Trithemius’s cipher procedure. ^4. arcani modus: literally “the mode/method of the hidden thing/secret,” i.e. the operating rule of the cipher. ^5. alphabetum usuale: the ordinary Latin alphabet used as the base sequence. ^6. ociosae: “idle,” i.e. null or unused intervening letters in the transposition scheme. ^7. OCR interlaceant is probably interiaceant, “lie between”; if printed as interlaceant, it may reflect a late/technical spelling, but the sense is the same. ^8. methatesis: metathesis, here letter-transposition; spelling reflects early-modern/Greek-derived technical vocabulary. ^9. tabula transpositionis recta: a “straight” transposition table, laid out as successive shifted rows. ^10. canonica: regular or rule-governed, not “canonical” in a theological sense. ^11. OCR sine repta is likely sine repetita or sine repetitione; the transmitted form is damaged, so the reconstruction is tentative. ^12. monogrammata: single-letter entries/signs in the table; the arithmetic treats table entries as countable letter-units.
